newsitem.title: FRANCE: FOCUS - French markets steady after post-poll dive.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - French markets steady after post-poll dive.

text.p: French markets steadied on Monday, reversing their initial dive after a Socialist-led parliamentary election victory, as investors nervously awaited new policy statements from the future government.

Socialist leader Lionel Jospin said President Jacques Chirac had asked him to be prime minister and told reporters he would form a government this week to take over from the outgoing centre-right coalition.

Analysts said after early steep losses on stocks and bonds, and a weakening in the franc against the mark, markets had reassessed the risks of a Socialist-led government and decided that, for now at least, they had said nothing to cause panic.
Socialist Party spokesman Francois Hollande said earlier the new government would carry out an audit of public finances in the next two weeks and make budget savings if necessary.

"The audit is important. It leaves the door open for backing off from rapid implementation of their programme," Merrill Lynch bond analyst Joanne Perez said. "Most of the emphasis on policy will be to reallocate spending."

Economists said Germany's own problems in dealing with its budget deficit and a political row there over a planned revaluation of central bank gold meant there was no reason to buy the German mark over the French franc, or German bonds over their French equivalents.
The franc strengthened to 3.3730 per mark after earlier touching a low of 3.3860.
Yields on French government bonds (OATs) also recovered to trade around 11 basis points below those in Germany, compared to three basis points below earlier on Monday.

The so-called Bund/OAT spread is a key barometer of how markets assess French investments relative to those in Germany and a negative spread can suggest that markets believe there is less risk in France than in Germany.
Economists, however, said investors were more likely to shift out of Europe altogether in favour of the dollar, given jitters about the continent's plans to launch a single currency in 1999.
"There is no reason to revalue Germany versus France. Europe in general is a much less safe bet," Perez said.
"It adds weight to the sell Europe story...but not France against Germany," Mark Capelton, international economist at BZW Ltd, said.

The stock market, seen as the most vulnerable to a left-wing victory given likely Socialist opposition to privatisations and company lay-offs, also clawed back into positive territory, before dipping again.
The CAC-40 blue-chip index was down 0.56 percent at 2,569.50 at 1137 GMT after plunging nearly three percent at the opening.
"The market has given its first verdict," one stock market trader said. But he said the market would be jumpy ahead of policy announcements from the new government.
"It is not at all guaranteed that this reaction can be sustained in the coming weeks," he added.
